identification.summary: China-based nation-state activity group that Microsoft tracks as the primary threat group targeting nations that ring the South China Sea [S1][S2]. Microsoft reports that it consistently targets government ministries, military entities, and corporate entities connected to critical infrastructure, particularly telecoms, and that it has been particularly persistent since January 2023 [S1]. In June 2023 it successfully targeted military and executive entities in Indonesia and a Malaysian maritime system [S2]. Microsoft maps APT30, LotusBlossom and LOTUS PANDA to Raspberry Typhoon [S3]; vendor reporting under those names describes Southeast Asia-focused espionage going back to at least 2005 (FireEye, APT30) [S5] and continuing into 2025-2026 (Cisco Talos, Symantec and Rapid7 reporting on Lotus Blossom / Lotus Panda) [S8][S9][S10].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft does not state a first-observed date [S1][S2]. FireEye said APT30 had been conducting cyber espionage since at least 2005 [S5]. Cisco Talos said Lotus Blossom has conducted espionage since at least 2012 [S8]; coverage of the Rapid7 reporting says Lotus Blossom has been active since 2009 [S10].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Raspberry Typhoon (formerly RADIUM) [S1][S3]. Microsoft's public naming map lists RADIUM, LOTUS PANDA, LotusBlossom and APT30 as other names for Raspberry Typhoon without naming the vendor for each [S3]. Microsoft does not map Naikon, Spring Dragon, Billbug/Thrip or PLA Unit 78020 to Raspberry Typhoon [S3]; Symantec, however, treats Billbug, Lotus Blossom and Thrip as one group [S7], and press coverage of Talos lists Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon and Thrip as Lotus Blossom aliases [S8]. MITRE tracks APT30 (G0013), Naikon (G0019), Lotus Blossom (G0030) and Thrip (G0076) as separate groups [S4]. Facts below are labelled by the reporting vendor's cluster name; do not assume every event is inside Microsoft's Raspberry Typhoon boundary.

attribution.sponsor: China. Microsoft describes Raspberry Typhoon as a nation-state activity group based out of China [S2]. FireEye assessed APT30 activity as state sponsored, most likely by the Chinese government [S5]. Talos describes Lotus Blossom as China-backed [S8]. No specific sponsoring organization (MSS or PLA) is named for the Microsoft cluster in the sources reviewed.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes activity to Raspberry Typhoon by name without a stated confidence level [S1][S2]. FireEye: 'most likely' Chinese government (2015) [S5]. Unit 42: likely nation-state sponsored, country not named (2015) [S6]. Talos: high confidence that the 2025-reported campaigns are Lotus Blossom, based on exclusive use of Sagerunex [S8]. Symantec (2025): Chinese actors, with attribution to a single actor not determined, though indicators linked to Billbug [S9]. Rapid7: medium confidence that Lotus Blossom compromised Notepad++ update infrastructure [S10]. No government attribution of the Microsoft-defined cluster was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry in its East Asia reports [S1][S2] and naming map [S3]; vendor malware and infrastructure analysis by FireEye [S5], Palo Alto Unit 42 [S6], Symantec [S7][S9], Cisco Talos [S8] and Rapid7 [S10], mostly reviewed through press coverage.

objectives: Long-term intelligence collection on governments, militaries and critical-infrastructure entities in South China Sea littoral and wider Southeast Asian states, consistent with Chinese strategic goals in the South China Sea [S1][S2]. FireEye described APT30 as focused on targets holding key political, economic and military information about the region, with activity spikes around ASEAN meetings [S5]. Microsoft's 2024 report places June 2023 Indonesia and Malaysia activity in the weeks before a rare multilateral naval exercise involving Indonesia, China and the United States [S2]. Symantec raised the concern that a compromised certificate authority could let the group sign malware with valid certificates [S7].

sectors: Government ministries, including defense, intelligence, economic and trade ministries [S1][S9]
Aviation: air traffic control and air freight [S9]
Manufacturing, media and news agencies, construction [S8][S9]
Journalists and commercial organizations with regional information [S5]
regions: Nations ringing the South China Sea [S1]
Unnamed Southeast Asian countries (2024-2025 Symantec reporting) [S9]
India and wider Southeast Asia (APT30 coverage) [S5]
Central America (per coverage of Rapid7 reporting) [S10]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's 2024 report lists Raspberry Typhoon with Flax Typhoon and Granite Typhoon as actors behind observed events in or around the South China Sea [S2]. Regions and sectors beyond S1-S2 come from vendor clusters that Microsoft maps (APT30, LotusBlossom, LOTUS PANDA) [S3] or that Symantec equates with Lotus Blossom (Billbug) [S7].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft says Raspberry Typhoon typically conducts intelligence collection and malware execution against government and infrastructure targets [S1]. APT30 used a sustained, planned malware development effort, including tools able to reach air-gapped networks, according to FireEye coverage [S5]; MITRE's G0013 software list includes BACKSPACE, NETEAGLE, SHIPSHAPE, SPACESHIP and FLASHFLOOD [S4]. Lotus Blossom used spearphishing with decoy documents (reportedly CVE-2012-0158) to deliver the Elise backdoor [S6]. Symantec tied the 2022 activity to the Hannotog and Sagerunex backdoors [S7]. Talos reports Sagerunex variants that use Dropbox, Twitter and Zimbra webmail as C2 tunnels instead of VPS servers [S8]. Symantec's 2025 reporting describes DLL sideloading through legitimate Trend Micro and Bitdefender binaries, ChromeKatz and CredentialKatz browser credential stealers, a reverse SSH tool, and a timestamp-altering utility (datechanger.exe) [S9]. Rapid7 reports a hijacked Notepad++ update path delivering a trojanized NSIS installer that sideloaded via a renamed Bitdefender binary to launch the Chrysalis backdoor [S10].

campaigns.name: APT30 decade-long espionage operation (FireEye report)
campaigns.summary: FireEye reported an operation dating to at least 2005 against government and commercial targets holding regional political, economic and military information in Southeast Asia and India, with activity around ASEAN meetings and air-gap-capable tooling.

campaigns.name: Operation Lotus Blossom (Unit 42)
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 linked more than 50 attacks over about three years against government and military organizations in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia using the Elise backdoor delivered by spearphishing.

campaigns.name: Billbug targeting of an Asian certificate authority
campaigns.summary: Symantec reported Billbug activity from March 2022 against a certificate authority, a government organization and defense agencies in Asia, using Hannotog and Sagerunex; no evidence certificates were compromised.

campaigns.name: Sustained South China Sea targeting
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports Raspberry Typhoon has been particularly persistent since January 2023 against government, military and telecom-linked critical-infrastructure targets around the South China Sea.

campaigns.name: Indonesia and Malaysia targeting before multilateral naval exercise
campaigns.summary: Raspberry Typhoon successfully targeted military and executive entities in Indonesia and a Malaysian maritime system in the weeks before a rare naval exercise involving Indonesia, China and the United States.

campaigns.name: Southeast Asia government, aviation and telecom intrusions (Symantec, Lotus Panda)
campaigns.summary: From August 2024 to February 2025, intrusions hit a government ministry, an air traffic control organization, a telecom operator and a construction company in one Southeast Asian country, plus a news agency and an air freight organization elsewhere in the region, using sideloading and Chrome credential stealers.

campaigns.name: Sagerunex campaigns in the Philippines, Vietnam, Hong Kong and Taiwan (Talos)
campaigns.summary: Talos reported Lotus Blossom campaigns against government, manufacturing, telecommunications and media organizations using Sagerunex variants with cloud-service C2.

campaigns.name: Notepad++ update infrastructure hijack (Chrysalis)
campaigns.summary: Rapid7 attributed, with medium confidence, a June-December 2025 compromise of Notepad++ hosting/update traffic to Lotus Blossom, used to deliver the Chrysalis backdoor to selected users; publicly reported February 2026.

diamond.adversary: China-based nation-state activity group (Microsoft: Raspberry Typhoon, formerly RADIUM) [S1][S2][S3]; overlapping vendor clusters APT30, Lotus Blossom/Lotus Panda and Billbug [S3][S5][S7][S8].
diamond.capability: Spearphishing with decoy documents and Elise [S6]; APT30 malware families [S4][S5]; Sagerunex and Hannotog backdoors [S7][S8]; DLL sideloading, Chrome credential stealers and reverse SSH [S9]; software-update hijacking delivering Chrysalis [S10].
diamond.infrastructure: Sagerunex C2 tunnelled through Dropbox, Twitter and Zimbra webmail instead of the earlier VPS servers [S8]; compromised Notepad++ hosting used to redirect update traffic to attacker-controlled downloads [S10].
diamond.victim: Government ministries, military, executive and defense entities, telecoms, maritime systems, aviation, certificate authorities and media in South China Sea and Southeast Asian states [S1][S2][S6][S7][S8][S9]; Notepad++ users selected for redirection [S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection that mirrors Chinese strategic goals in the South China Sea, timed around ASEAN meetings and a multilateral naval exercise involving the United States [S1][S2][S5].
diamond.technology: Government and military Windows networks, telecom and aviation infrastructure, PKI/certificate services, cloud services abused for C2, and software update mechanisms [S2][S7][S8][S9][S10].

gaps: Primary documents could not be opened: FireEye APT30 report (2015), Unit 42 Operation Lotus Blossom, Symantec Billbug (2022) and Lotus Panda (2025) blogs, Cisco Talos Lotus Blossom blog, Rapid7 Chrysalis report, Kaspersky Naikon/Spring Dragon and MITRE pages; content is drawn from search-result summaries and press coverage.

Cluster boundaries are unresolved. Microsoft maps only RADIUM, LOTUS PANDA, LotusBlossom and APT30 [S3]; MITRE keeps APT30, Naikon, Lotus Blossom and Thrip separate [S4]. Symantec merges Billbug/Thrip with Lotus Blossom [S7]. Naikon (and its PLA Unit 78020 attribution) is not verified as part of Raspberry Typhoon.

Microsoft has not publicly tied the 2025 Sagerunex, 2024-2025 Symantec or Notepad++ activity to Raspberry Typhoon by name; those links rest on Microsoft's alias mapping plus vendor attributions of differing confidence (Symantec could not pin the 2025 activity to a single actor; Rapid7 medium confidence).
Exact publication dates for the Talos (2025-03) and Rapid7 (2026-02) reports were taken from coverage, not the primary pages.
No sponsoring organization (MSS vs PLA) is named for the Microsoft cluster; no government attribution found.
Victims of the Notepad++ redirection and specific Raspberry Typhoon victim organizations after 2023 are not public in reviewed sources.
The claim of Central America targeting appears only in secondary coverage [S10] and is unverified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (Operational environment): Key terrain includes partner-nation government ministries, military and executive networks, telecom carriers, maritime and aviation systems, PKI providers, and software update channels in South China Sea littoral states [S1][S2][S7][S9][S10]. STEP 2 (Effects): Coalition and exercise planning shared with these partners is exposed through partner networks, and activity has been timed before multilateral naval exercises and ASEAN meetings [S2][S5]. STEP 3 (Threat model): spearphishing or trusted-software update hijack, DLL sideloading of signed security-vendor binaries, Sagerunex/Chrysalis-class backdoors with C2 over Dropbox, Twitter or Zimbra, browser credential theft and timestamp tampering [S6][S8][S9][S10]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent, quiet collection from partner defense and foreign ministries and telecoms ahead of regional exercises and diplomatic events [S1][S2][S5]. MDCOA is use of a compromised certificate authority or software update channel to sign or push implants into many networks, including those connected to US forces [S7][S10]. Candidate indicators: unexpected Trend Micro or Bitdefender binaries loading DLLs from unusual paths; workstation traffic to Dropbox/Twitter/Zimbra APIs from non-browser processes; GUP.exe or updater processes fetching installers from non-vendor IPs; ChromeKatz/CredentialKatz artifacts; file timestamp anomalies [S8][S9][S10].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: fuse partner-nation and vendor reporting on Lotus Blossom/Lotus Panda/APT30 under the Raspberry Typhoon name while keeping vendor cluster labels visible, since attributions vary in confidence [S3][S8][S9][S10]. Authorities: most victims are partner-nation government and telecom networks [S1][S2][S9], so response depends on partner agreements and defend-forward or hunt-forward authorities rather than DODIN-only actions. Mission assurance: exercise and coalition planning data shared with Southeast Asian partners, and software update and PKI trust used by mission systems, are at risk [S2][S7][S10]; validate update integrity for third-party tools on mission networks. Coordination: synchronize with partner CERTs, and with the security vendors whose binaries are abused for sideloading, before and during regional exercises [S2][S9].
